title: Provinciae Palestinae Liber De Fide [Incertus]
author: Rufinus Aquileiensis

passages.original: Quod autem diabolus, vel ejus qui dicuntur Angeli, de creaturis caelestibus sunt, 502 rationabilibusque virtutibus, testis est beatus Petrus, cum sic dicit, Si enim Deus Angelis qui peccaverunt non pepercit (2. Petr. 2. 4.). Similiter autem et beatus Paulus docet, dicens : Nescitis quoniam Angelos judicabimus (1. Cor. 6. 5.)? Ne quis igitur arbitretur captus errore, quod isti ante peccaverunt quam hominibus inviderent, et post il- lud peccatum ad decipiendos homines devenere, sic- ut nefarius Origenes docebat : sed ut superius dixi(??) ex eo quod diabolus in serpentem transfiguratus Evam decepit. Quod autem ex illo diabolus, veritate penitus derelicta transtulit se protinus ad mendacium, ex quo Evam, ut dixi, peremit morte peccati, testis est Dominus noster cum dicit Judaeis non credenti- bus sibi, Vos ex patre diabolo estis, desideria pa ris vestri diaboli Cultis facere.
passages.english: That the devil, or those who are called his angels, are from among the heavenly creatures and rational powers, blessed Peter is witness, when he says thus: "For if God did not spare the angels who sinned" (2 Pet. 2:4). And likewise blessed Paul also teaches, saying: "Do you not know that we shall judge angels?" (1 Cor. 6:3). Let no one, then, taken captive by error, suppose that these sinned before they envied men, and that after that sin they came down to deceive men, as the wicked Origen taught; but [rather], as I said above, [they sinned] from the fact that the devil, transformed into a serpent, deceived Eve. And that from that point the devil, having utterly abandoned the truth, at once passed over to falsehood, from the time when, as I said, he destroyed Eve by the death of sin, our Lord is witness when he says to the Jews who did not believe him: "You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father the devil."
passages.notes: The sentence beginning "but as I said above" is elliptical in the Latin; the bracketed words supply the apparent sense (the fall dates from the deception of Eve). "Cultis" read as "vultis" (scanning error); "pa ris" as "patris". The edition's reference 1 Cor. 6:5 is in fact 1 Cor. 6:3. The stray numbers 502 are page markers and are omitted.

passages.original: Quod amem Deus dimiserit eis pecca- tum, sicut etiam Cain qui primum peccaverat indul- sit, cum dixisset ad eum, Peccasti, quiesce : ad te re- versio ejus, hoc est peccati, et tu dominaberis ei (Gen. 4. 7.), aperte Moyses ostendit per humanitatem seu misericordiam, quam Deus ipsis postea libenter indulsit. Quid enim dicit Moyses? Et fecit Dominus Deus Adam et uxoris ejus tunicas pelliceas, et vestivit eos (Gen. 3. 12.). Nam si Dominus ipsis peccatum non dimisisset, nunquam profecto per semetipsum vestiret eos tunicis, a quibus illis ipse perfecerat. Ne quis igitur easdem pelliceas tunicas quas habuerunt, humanum corpus existimet, b sicut impius Origenes ex posuit. Nam ante istas quas dixi pelliceas tunicas ipse Adam carnem habere se docuit dicens. Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro de came mea (Gen. 2. 23.). Pelliceas igitur tun(??)cas datas a Deo fuisse dici- mus propter asperitatem vitae, vel quod tanquam se exercentibus ad virtutem 602 eas dabat quae con- gruae videbantur, ut discerent non aliter posse vin- cere invisibiles inimicos, nisi laboribus corporis.
passages.english: But that God forgave them their sin, just as he also pardoned Cain, who had first sinned, when he said to him, "You have sinned; be still: its return is to you", that is, of the sin, "and you shall rule over it" (Gen. 4:7), Moses plainly shows through the kindness or mercy which God afterwards willingly granted them. For what does Moses say? "And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife garments of skin, and clothed them" (Gen. 3:21). For if the Lord had not forgiven them their sin, he would certainly never have clothed them himself with garments, from which he himself had [already] provided for them. Let no one, then, suppose that those same garments of skin which they had were the human body, as the impious Origen expounded. For before these garments of skin of which I spoke, Adam himself showed that he had flesh, saying: "This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Gen. 2:23). We say, therefore, that garments of skin were given by God on account of the harshness of life, or because he was giving to them, as to people training themselves for virtue, those [garments] that seemed fitting, so that they might learn that they could not overcome their invisible enemies otherwise than by bodily labours.
passages.notes: "amem" read as "autem". The clause "a quibus illis ipse perfecerat" seems corrupt and its sense is uncertain; the rendering is tentative. The edition's reference Gen. 3:12 should be Gen. 3:21. The stray letter "b" (footnote mark) and the number 602 (page marker) are omitted.
